# Sarabhaṅgajātaka (Ja 522)
**ID:** Ja 522
**Section:** Jātaka (ja)

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
The *Sarabhaṅgajātaka* (Ja 522) is a birth story in the Pali Jātaka collection within the Khuddaka Nikāya [Appleton 2010; SuttaCentral]. According to the narrative frame, the Buddha related this story while dwelling at the Bamboo Grove concerning the death of the Elder Mahāmoggallāna [SuttaCentral; Keown 1996]. In the core legend, the Bodhisatta was born as the archer Jotipāla (later the sage Sarabhaṅga), renowned for his exceptional archery feats—such as shooting an iron arrow to defend against four archers, a display of martial arts referred to elsewhere in the Pali *Nidānakathā* to illustrate the Buddha's own youth [Murphy 2010; Gombrich 1991; Gaffney 2003; Fausböll 1897]. Later as the teacher Sarabhaṅga, he responds to doctrinal and moral inquiries posed by deities including Sakka, discoursing on patience with rough speech, the definition of the virtuous person (*sappurisa*), and the nature of the truly wise person [Anandajoti 2010]. In Jātakapāḷi editorial structure, Ja 522 is notable for including a verse connection (*samodhāna*) identifying the Buddha with the title *lokanātha* rather than using the standard term *bodhisatta* [Appleton 2010].
In text reuse and cross-tradition transmission, the Jātaka has a direct full parallel in the Lokottaravādin Mahāsāṅghika tradition preserved in the *Mahāvastu-avadāna* (*The Jātaka of Śarabhaṅga*, Mvu 99) [SuttaCentral; Norman 1997; DharmaNexus]. SuttaCentral also notes a passage-level parallel in the *Araññāyatanaisisutta* (SN 11.9) [SuttaCentral]. DharmaNexus aligns Ja 522 broadly with its own *Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā* commentary, the *Saddanītippakaraṇa*, the *Sakka Saṁyutta* (SN 11), and the *Devaputta Saṁyutta* (SN 2), alongside cross-language alignments with Sanskrit collections (*Mahāvastu*, *Udānavarga*), the Chinese *Saṃyuktāgama* (T 99), and Tibetan canonical parallels [DharmaNexus]. Scenes depicting the Bodhisatta Jotipāla's archery feat from the *Sarabhaṅgajātaka* have also been identified in Southeast Asian art, notably on 7th–12th-century Dvaravati Buddhist boundary markers (*sīmā*) from the Khorat Plateau [Murphy 2010].
